newsitem.title: UK: Analysts warn of rough ride ahead for BA.
newsitem.headline: Analysts warn of rough ride ahead for BA.

text.p: Shares in British Airways held firm on Tuesday despite warnings that its proposed alliance with American Airlines could run into trouble in its long flight to winning regulatory approvals in Europe and the United States.
BA's share price was up 2-1/2 pence at 603 pence, shrugging off fresh reports that the European Commission (EC) could clash with Britain over the legality of the deal.

But some analysts took a more cautious stance, warning that at best BA and American could face further delays in getting all the approvals needed on both sides of the Atlantic and in the process might have to make more concessions.
"I view the situation with a lot of caution. The hurdles are just so many and so political," said James Halstead, London-based airlines analyst with Credit Lyonnais.
"The trouble is that British Airways has always talked about this alliance as though it's a done deal," said another analyst, Nigel Davies of brokers Panmure Gordon.

"There is now a very big risk that BA will be left with a gap in its U.S. alliances this year," he said, referring to the fact that BA's divorce from its current transatlantic partner USAir is due to take effect from the end of March.

But BA remained optimistic on Tuesday that the deal would get done by this summer despite the conflict between Britain and the European Commission and the fact that the two airlines also have to win approvals from the U.S. authorities.

"The deal...is planned to be implemented during the course of the early summer of this year and I see no reason why it should not be possible to achieve that timetable," chief executive Robert Ayling told an interview on BBC radio news.

On Monday European Commission sources said competition commissioner Karel Van Miert had told British Trade Secretary Ian Lang that the Commission would not tolerate British approval of the BA/AA deal if it conflicted with the EC's own views.
He warned that the Commmission would defend its view in the European Court of Justice if necessary.

Asked how he felt about this apparent challenge by the EC against Britain's proposals to conditionally approve the deal, Ayling said, "I remain optimistic that we can get through this and get approval".

While Lang's Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) declined comment as it had not yet seen the letter, and had not yet given its own final ruling on the deal, Ayling said it was too early to say the regulators would end up in conflict.

Lang proposed in December conditions for allowing the alliance to go ahead, including a demand that the companies release a total of 168 weekly runway slots at London Heathrow to make room for more competition.

But according to one EU source, Van Miert said in his letter 168 slots would not be enough to ensure adequate competition -- the EC would want a figure nearer 300-400 and these slots would have to be surrendered, not sold.
Ayling said he thought the commissioner's reported claims that the plan would substantially restrict competition on all routes between Britain and the U.S. were unfounded.

"Karel Van Miert's analysis is based on the assumption that there will be no new air services agreement between Britain and the United States whereas we, the British government and the American government, have all made it clear that there had to be open skies agreement," he said.
Ayling said BA and AMR Corp's American had made clear that their entire plan was conditional on an open skies agreement being sealed between Britain and the U.S.
In addition, he said, it seemed to soon to predict the regulators' final positions.
